title: The Lahore Sabha, 1879
hookLine: a bolder reform society formed in Lahore

lines: A YOUNG TEACHER AND HIS FRIENDS.
cards: Lahore, the old capital of Ranjit Singh's kingdom, is now a British city of colleges, printing presses and newspapers.
A young teacher at a college there, and a circle of friends around him, have been watching the Amritsar Sabha. They agree with its aims. But they think it's too polite.
Too careful with old privileges. Too slow to say plainly what the Gurus said. So they start their own.

teach.b: First, who they were. The Lahore Singh Sabha gathered teachers, clerks and writers, people who lived by books and print.
Professor Gurmukh Singh was among its leaders, and Giani Ditt Singh, a writer you'll meet tomorrow, joined it. Second, what they said out loud.
All Sikhs are equal before the Guru, whatever family they were born into. No one is owed special honor in the sangat for descending from a Guru's family. Caste has no place at the Guru's door.
In a hymn in Sri Rag, Guru Nanak says he stands with the lowest of the low, and has no wish to vie with the great. The Lahore reformers took that line at its word. Third, the clash.

The Amritsar leaders included men of honored lineages, some descended from the Gurus' own families, who held that old customs and old respect deserved a place. The Lahore group thought this blurred the Gurus' teaching.

The two Sabhas formed rival councils, and their disagreement was public and sometimes bitter. Each side believed it was protecting the Panth. Historians still weigh both sides, and this lesson leaves the judging to them.
The Lahore reformers spoke clearly in print: papers and pamphlets in Punjabi, passed from hand to hand. A sentence on a page could travel further than a speech in a hall.
Speaking clearly isn't shouting. It means saying the thing plainly, so nobody has to guess what you meant.

how: Sikhs remember the Lahore Singh Sabha for its plain insistence, in Punjabi papers and pamphlets, that all Sikhs stand equal before the Guru whatever their birth.

games.q: you're a Lahore teacher. you agree with Amritsar's aims but think it's too careful. what do you do?
o: start your own Sabha and speak plainly in print.
games.why: the Lahore group formed its own Sabha and pressed equality before the Guru through papers and pamphlets.

practice: Think of something that matters to you that you've been saying in a roundabout way, or not at all: a need, a thanks, a boundary.
Let the extra words fall away one by one until a single plain sentence is left, and breathe with it; it doesn't need to be sharp, just clear. If you pray, rest in Waheguru between the breaths.

wordCard.voice: Sabha, an assembly or society: the bolder Lahore Singh Sabha, which said plainly in print that all Sikhs stand equal before the Guru. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: speak clearly. Plain words, kindly said, travel far. That's day nine hundred sixty-two.
